newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil moves to secure dollar reserves.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil moves to secure dollar reserves.

text.p: Brazil cut a host of taxes for foreign investors on Friday, hoping to lure dollars to pad international reserves amid growing concern over a widening current account balance of payments gap, economists said.

"This is a measure that is aimed at creating a comfortable level of reserves to be ready for whatever might happen in the future," said Alcindo Ferreira, a former Central Bank official and consultant for Trend Analise.

The Central Bank said in a statement that it was cutting financial transaction taxes, known as the IOF, on fixed-income funds and non-resident accounts to two percent from seven percent. Also, it eliminated taxes on all foreign borrowing.
"The idea is to ensure the continuity of (dollar) flows," Central Bank President Gustavo Loyola told InvestNews agency, adding he did not think the changes would lead to a flood of new money.

It was the government's second move in as many weeks to entice foreign investors to keep their money in Brazil, or bring in more. On April 16, the Central Bank ended an eight-month pattern of interest rate cuts and left rates unchanged, fearing further cuts could reduce capital flows.

Economists say the Central Bank wants to keep reserves at the $58 billion level, especially when rising U.S. interest rates threaten to redirect capital flows needed to finance Brazil's current account deficit.
The current account deficit, expected to top $30 billion in 1997, is being pressured by a burgeoning trade gap that economists say will hit at least $10 billion this year.

"The tax cuts are positive because they show the government is intent and proactive in keeping reserves at current levels. On the negative side, it is just another palliative measure because it is not going to effect the fundamentals," said Mauro Schneider, chief economist at ING Bank in Brazil.

Schneider and others said significant improvement in the current account, trade and fiscal deficits will only come in the medium- to long-term after a number of constitutional reforms are approved by Congress.

The new tax rules did not entirely surprise the markets, which have grown accustomed to minor tinkering by the government since late March, when the Central Bank imposed tougher import financing measures to curb the trade gap.
And most Brazil watchers think the government's next move will be to slap on additional credit restrictions for the purchase of specific products as part of an ongoing bid to curb imports.

The tax changes were not expected to have any effect on the Brazilian stock market because taxes on equity investments remained at zero percent. But traders saw increasing dollar flows, especially into the floating interbank market, where the tax fell to two percent from seven percent.

A foreign exchange director at a leading Rio de Janeiro investment bank said the measure would boost total foreign reserves to over $60 billion within two months, but others said the forecast was a bit optimistic.

The tax changes were also expected to increase the number of Eurobond issues by smaller companies that can only launch short-dated paper of no more than three-years. Now they will pay no tax, whereas before they faced a three percent duty.
"That's a big savings, $3 million on a $100 million deal," said a Eurobond trader in Sao Paulo.
